entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17093"/><div sID="gen33859" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17093"/><hi type="bold">6. five hundred--</hi>This appearance was probably on the mountain (Tabor, according to tradition), in Galilee, when His most solemn and public appearance, according to His special promise, was vouchsafed (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.32">Mt 26:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.28.7">28:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.16">10, 16</reference>). He "appointed" this place, as one remote from Jerusalem, so that believers might assemble there more freely and securely. Alford's theory of Jerusalem being the scene, is improbable; as such a multitude of believers could not, with any safety, have met in one place in the metropolis, after His crucifixion there. The number of disciples (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.15">Ac 1:15</reference>) at Jerusalem shortly after, was one hundred and twenty, those in Galilee and elsewhere not being reckoned. Andronicus and Junius were, perhaps, of the number (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.7">Ro 16:7</reference>): they are said to be "among the apostles" (who all were witnesses of the resurrection, <reference osisRef="Acts.1.22">Ac 1:22</reference>).<div eID="gen33859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33860" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remain unto this present--</hi>and, therefore, may be sifted thoroughly to ascertain the trustworthiness of their testimony.<div eID="gen33860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33861" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fallen asleep--</hi>in the sure hope of awaking at the resurrection (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.60">Ac 7:60</reference>). <div eID="gen33861" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17095"/><div sID="gen33864" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17095"/><hi type="bold">8. One born out of due time--</hi>Greek, "the one abortively born": the abortion in the family of the apostles. As a child born before the due time is puny, and though born alive, yet not of the proper size, and scarcely worthy of the name of man, so "I am the least of the apostles," scarcely "meet to be called an apostle"; a supernumerary taken into the college of apostles out of regular course, not led to Christ by long instruction, like a natural birth, but by a sudden power, as those prematurely born [Grotius]. Compare the similar image from childbirth, and by the same spiritual power, the resurrection of Christ (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.3">1Pe 1:3</reference>). "Begotten again by the resurrection of Jesus." Jesus' appearance to Paul, on the way to Damascus, is the one here referred to. <div eID="gen33864" type="x-p"/>

Then--</hi>after that: next in the succession of "orders" or "ranks."<div eID="gen33891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33892" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the end--</hi>the general resurrection, and final judgment and consummation (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.46">Mt 25:46</reference>).<div eID="gen33892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">delivered up ... kingdom to ... Father--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="John.13.3">Joh 13:3</reference>). Seeming at variance with <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">Da 7:14</reference>, "His dominion is an everlasting dominion which shall not pass away." Really, His giving up of the mediatorial kingdom to the Father, when the end for which the mediatorial economy was established has been accomplished, is altogether in harmony with its continuing everlastingly. The change which shall then take place, shall be in the manner of administration, not in the kingdom itself; God shall then come into direct connection with the earth, instead of mediatorially, when Christ shall have fully and finally removed everything that severs asunder the holy God and a sinful earth (<reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col 1:20</reference>). The glory of God is the final end of Christ's mediatorial office (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.10">Php 2:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.11">11</reference>). His co-equality with the Father is independent of the latter, and prior to it, and shall, therefore, continue when its function shall have ceased. His manhood, too, shall everlastingly continue, though, as now, subordinate to the Father. The throne of the Lamb (but no longer mediatorial) as well as of God, shall be in the heavenly city (<reference osisRef="Rev.22.3">Re 22:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Re 3:21</reference>). The unity of the Godhead, and the unity of the Church, shall be simultaneously manifested at Christ's second coming. Compare <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.9">Zep 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.14.9">Zec 14:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.21-John.17.24">Joh 17:21-24</reference>. The oldest manuscripts for "shall have delivered up," read, "delivereth up," which suits the sense better. It is "when He shall have put down all rule," that "He delivereth up the kingdom to the Father."<div eID="gen33893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall have put down all rule--</hi>the effect produced during the millennary reign of Himself and His saints (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Psa 110:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.8.6">8:6</reference>; 2:6-9), to which passages Paul refers, resting his argument on the two words, "all" and "until," of the Psalmist: a proof of verbal inspiration of Scripture (compare <reference osisRef="Rev.2.26">Re 2:26</reference>, 27). Meanwhile, He "rules in the midst of His enemies" (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.2">Psa 110:2</reference>). He is styled "the King" when He takes His great power (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.34">Mt 25:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.15">Re 11:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.11.17">17</reference>). The Greek for "put down" is, "done away with," or "brought to naught." "All" must be subject to Him, whether openly opposed powers, as Satan and his angels, or kings and angelic principalities (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.21">Ep 1:21</reference>). <div eID="gen33894" type="x-p"/>

How--</hi>It is folly to deny a fact of REVELATION, because we do not know the "how." Some measure God's power by their petty intelligence, and won't admit, even on His assurance, anything which they cannot explain. Ezekiel's answer of faith to the question is the truly wise one (<reference osisRef="Ezek.37.3">Eze 37:3</reference>). So Jesus argues not on principles of philosophy, but wholly from "the power of God," as declared by the Word of God (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.26">Mt 19:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.10.27">Mr 10:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.12.23">12:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.18.27">Lu 18:27</reference>).<div eID="gen33921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33922" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come--</hi>The dead are said to depart, or to be deceased: those rising again to come. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17123"/><div sID="gen33923" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17123"/><hi type="bold">36. fool--</hi>with all thy boasted philosophy (<reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">Psa 14:1</reference>).<div eID="gen33923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33924" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that which thou--</hi>"thou," emphatical: appeal to the objector's own experience: "The seed which thou thyself sowest." Paul, in this verse and in <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.42">1Co 15:42</reference>, answers the question of <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.35">1Co 15:35</reference>, "How?" and in 1Co 15:37-41, 43, the question, "With what kind of body?" He converts the very objection (the death of the natural body) into an argument. Death, so far from preventing quickening, is the necessary prelude and prognostication of it, just as the seed "is not quickened" into a new sprout with increased produce, "except it die" (except a dissolution of its previous organization takes place). Christ by His death for us has not given us a reprieve from death as to the life which we have from Adam; nay, He permits the law to take its course on our fleshly nature; but He brings from Himself new spiritual and heavenly life out of death (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.37">1Co 15:37</reference>). <div eID="gen33924" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17124"/><div sID="gen33925" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17124"/><hi type="bold">37. not that body that shall be--</hi>a body beautiful and no longer a "bare grain" [Bengel]. No longer without stalk or ear, but clothed with blade and ears, and yielding many grains instead of only one [Grotius]. There is not an identity of all the particles of the old and the new body. For the perpetual transmutation of matter is inconsistent with this. But there is a hidden germ which constitutes the identity of body amidst all outward changes: the outward accretions fall off in its development, while the germ remains the same. Every such germ ("seed," <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.38">1Co 15:38</reference>) "shall have its own body," and be instantly recognized, just as each plant now is known from the seed that was sown (see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.13">1Co 6:13</reference>). So Christ by the same image illustrated the truth that His death was the necessary prelude of His putting on His glorified body, which is the ground of the regeneration of the many who believe (<reference osisRef="John.12.24">Joh 12:24</reference>). Progress is the law of the spiritual, as of the natural world. Death is the avenue not to mere revivification or reanimation, but to resurrection and regeneration (<reference osisRef="Matt.19.28">Mt 19:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.21">Php 3:21</reference>). Compare "planted," &c., <reference osisRef="Rom.6.5">Ro 6:5</reference>. <div eID="gen33925" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv17133"/><div sID="gen33949" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv17133"/><hi type="bold">46. afterward--</hi>Adam had a soul not necessarily mortal, as it afterwards became by sin, but "a living soul," and destined to live for ever, if he had eaten of the tree of life (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.22">Ge 3:22</reference>); still his body was but an animal-souled body, not a spiritual body, such as believers shall have; much less was he a "life-giving spirit," as Christ. Or the Spirit by Paul hints that the other trumpets mentioned subsequently in the Apocalypse shall precede, and that this shall be the last of all (compare Is 27:13 ; Zec 9:14 ). Quoted from <reference osisRef="Hos.13.14">Ho 13:14</reference>, substantially; but freely used by the warrant of the Spirit by which Paul wrote. The Hebrew may be translated, "O death, where are thy plagues? Where, O Hades, is thy destruction?" The Septuagint, "Where is thy victory (literally, in a lawsuit), O death? Where is thy sting, O Hades? ... Sting" answers to the Hebrew "plagues," namely, a poisoned sting causing plagues. Appropriate, as to the old serpent (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.14">Ge 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.21.6">Nu 21:6</reference>). "Victory" answers to the Hebrew "destruction." Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.25.7">Is 25:7</reference>, "destroy ... veil ... over all nations," namely, victoriously destroy it; and to "in victory" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.54">1Co 15:54</reference>), which he triumphantly repeats. The "where" implies their past victorious destroying power and sting, now gone for ever; obtained through Satan's triumph over man in Eden, which enlisted God's law on the side of Satan and death against man (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.12">Ro 5:12</reference>, 17, 21). The souls in Hades being freed by the resurrection, death's sting and victory are gone. For "O grave," the oldest manuscripts and versions read, "O death," the second time. <div eID="gen33971" type="x-p"/>

navigation_sections.content_plain: CHAPTER 15 1Co 15:1-58 . The Resurrection Proved against the Deniers of It at Corinth. Christ's resurrection rests on the evidence of many eye-witnesses, including Paul himself, and is the great fact preached as the groundwork of the Gospel: they who deny the resurrection in general, must deny that of Christ, and the consequence of the latter will be, that Christian preaching and faith are vain.
